title: AI-Generated Content Tells
skill:
# Dead Giveaways of AI-Generated Marketing Copy

A practical reference for spotting — and not writing — machine-sounding prose.

> **Read this first.** There is *no deterministic way* to prove a piece of writing is AI-generated. LLMs learned from humans, so every individual signal produces false positives: plenty of careful writers use em-dashes and tricolons. **It's the *cluster* of tells together that's diagnostic, never any single one.** Treat everything below as evidence to weigh, not proof — and when writing, count the cluster rather than banning one symbol.

---

## The em-dash myth (start here)

The em-dash is the most-cited "tell" and one of the weakest. Em-dashes show up in AI output because the humans who wrote the training data used them — they've been a staple of journalism and literature for centuries. By itself, punctuation is not a reliable marker, and detection tools regularly flag authentic human writing as AI partly on this basis.

The real tells are **structural and rhythmic**, not about any single word or symbol. Use the em-dash as circumstantial context at most.

---

## Structural & rhythmic tells (strongest)

- **The rule of three, everywhere.** Tricolons like "fast, reliable, and scalable," parallel triplets repeated across paragraphs and section after section.
- **"It's not just X, it's Y"** antithesis constructions, and **"From X to Y"** framings.
- **Negative parallelism:** "This isn't about… it's about…"
- **Uniform cadence.** Sentences and paragraphs of suspiciously even length — none of the awkward long-or-short variation humans naturally produce. Every section opening with the same move (a scene-setter, then a pivot, then a promise).
- **Perfectly parallel lists.** Every bullet the same length, opening with the same part of speech, closing on the same beat. Real lists are ragged.
- **Summary sentences that restate the paragraph** that just ran, adding nothing.
- **Relentless signposting.** "Let's dive in," "Here's the thing," "The bottom line," plus tidy intro → body → conclusion structure even for two lines.
- **Over-balanced framing.** "On one hand / on the other" with no actual position taken.

## Vocabulary tells

- **Overused verbs/nouns:** *delve, leverage (as a verb), navigate, foster, underscore, harness, elevate, unlock, tapestry, realm, landscape, testament, crucial, pivotal, robust, seamless.*
- **Hollow hype:** *world-class, game-changing, best-in-class, cutting-edge, at the heart of, in today's fast-paced…*
- **Hedging-plus-summary closers:** "Ultimately," "In conclusion," "It's worth noting that."
- **Hollow engagement phrases:** "Great question!", "I hope this helps!"

## Texture tells

- **Too clean.** Spotless, evenly-groomed prose with no idiosyncrasy.
- **Emoji-bulleted lists** with bold lead-ins (✅ **Benefit:** …).
- **Confident vagueness.** Many words, few specifics, no stake, no number, no named thing.

### The 5-second test
Sterile rhythm + repetitive transitions + zero personality = likely AI.

---

## Writing this page without the tells

This is hospitality account-based-marketing prose: a proposal page written to one named company about its own event calendar and where its people will sleep, meet, and work. The tells above are exactly what such a page drifts into, because the subject matter invites adjectives. Concrete practice:

- **Name things instead of praising them.** "Twelve minutes on the Central line from Stratford" beats "conveniently located". A hotel name, a distance, a room count, a date, a venue — every one of those does more work than an adjective.
- **Vary the rhythm on purpose.** Let one sentence run and the next be four words. If two adjacent paragraphs have the same shape, break one.
- **At most one tricolon on the whole page**, if any. Prefer two items, or four, or a list that doesn't balance.
- **Ragged bullets.** No list where every item opens with the same part of speech or lands on the same length. Mix a three-word item with a twelve-word one.
- **Cut the summary sentence.** If a sentence restates the paragraph above it, delete it; the reader already read it.
- **No "not just X, it's Y", no "from X to Y", no "this isn't about… it's about…"** anywhere.
- **No hollow intensifiers.** If removing the adjective doesn't change the meaning, remove the adjective.
- **Say the awkward specific.** Real proposals admit constraints — a shuttle at peak times, a walk that's ten minutes not five. Specificity is what reads as human.
- **Em-dashes are fine in moderation.** They are not the tell. The cluster is: even cadence *plus* tricolons *plus* hype vocabulary *plus* parallel bullets. Fix those, and the punctuation takes care of itself.

**Self-review pass:** re-read the finished copy once looking only for this cluster — tricolons, identical paragraph lengths, hype words, parallel bullets, restating closers — and rewrite what you find before shipping.

---

## Quick-Reference

| | |
|---|---|
| **Fastest tell** | Sterile, even rhythm |
| **Most durable tell** | Tricolons + "not just X, it's Y" + signposting |
| **Don't rely on** | Em-dashes alone |

**The one rule that always holds:** a single tell means little. A cluster of them is what actually convicts.
skill_sementics: Use when writing, editing, or reviewing marketing and proposal copy to keep it from reading as AI-generated. Covers the structural, rhythmic, vocabulary and texture tells of machine-written prose, the weakness of the em-dash as a signal, and a concrete checklist for writing hospitality / account-based-marketing pages without those tells. Apply whenever drafting on-page copy or doing a self-review pass before publishing. The core principle: no single signal is proof; only a cluster of tells is diagnostic.
